title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
gist: Damodaran shows US equities held up through a 54bp September jump in the 10-year to 5.29% because AI capex is converting into supplier earnings (Q2 2026 aggregate earnings +57% y/y), while free cash flow and shareholder payouts lag; he frames four investor stances on AI and goes with market consensus plus extra cash.

insights.claim: The US 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.75% to 5.29% in September 2026, a 54bp monthly move that ranks in the top ten percent of 770 monthly changes since 1962.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Rate shock of this size normally pressures equities; the fact it did not is the signal.
insights.quote: The September rise in rates would put in the top ten percent of 770 monthly rate changes

insights.claim: US equities added $2.5 trillion of market cap in September 2026 despite the rate spike, with almost $1.5 trillion coming from technology.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Index strength is concentrated in tech, so aggregate resilience overstates breadth.

insights.claim: Market gains in 2026 are narrow: technology, energy and materials carried the market, only about 50% of companies in each sector are up for the year, and about 65% of listed stocks fell in the third quarter.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Divergence under the index; stock-picking and breadth matter more than the headline.

insights.claim: Damodaran's implied equity risk premium fell below 4% for the first time in 2026, to 3.70% over the 10-year (3.92% over his dollar riskfree rate), even as implied expected equity returns rose from 8.41% to 8.99%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Equities are being priced to a thinner cushion over Treasuries; lower ERP signals pricier stocks.

insights.claim: Stocks have absorbed higher rates because higher-than-expected 2026 earnings and rising 2027-28 earnings expectations offset the higher discount rate, rather than because of a falling risk premium.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Equity resilience depends on earnings delivery; an earnings miss would expose the rate sensitivity.

insights.claim: AI capex is a transfer between public companies: hyperscaler spending depresses their earnings and free cash flow, but becomes revenue and profit for chipmakers, network gear, power producers and data-center real estate firms.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Trade the supplier side of the capex chain for current earnings; builders carry the payback risk.

insights.claim: US public company capex in Q2 2026 was up $133.4 billion, almost 36%, versus Q2 2025, with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary each growing more than 50%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Capex growth is concentrated in the AI builders' sectors.

insights.claim: Between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026 US book equity rose about 13% ($1.8 trillion) and total debt about 8% ($1.9 trillion); technology saw book equity up almost 30% and debt up about 18.8%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Debt-funded AI buildout is raising leverage in the very sector that dominates the index.

insights.claim: Longer amortization schedules at the AI builders are reducing the current earnings hit from capex, flattering reported earnings while the cash is already spent.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Watch for depreciation-life assumptions as an earnings-quality flag.

insights.claim: Aggregate US net income rose from $511bn to $692bn (+35%) in Q1 2026 and from $576bn to $904bn (+57%) in Q2 2026 year on year, but more than half of companies reported falling net income.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Earnings boom is narrow, led by tech, financials and communication services; health care, utilities and real estate lag.

insights.claim: Public-company data understate AI's true leverage because private players such as Anthropic and OpenAI, and off-balance-sheet joint ventures, are missing from the figures.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: True AI debt and capital intensity is larger than public statements show.

insights.claim: LTM dividends rose about $43.3bn (5%) and buybacks about $106.7bn (9%) versus calendar 2025, well behind earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Earnings growth is not converting into shareholder cash at the same rate.

insights.claim: S&P 500 companies returned only 63% of earnings to shareholders in the last twelve months, the lowest since 2004, versus 80%+ for most of two decades, because AI capex absorbs free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Lower payout ratio means earnings overstate distributable cash; supports caution on buyback-driven support for prices.
insights.locator: cash returned as a percent of earnings

insights.claim: If AI delivers, investors get a more capital-intensive set of winners with returns above cost of capital and lenders repaid; if AI fails, expect capex write-offs, price markdowns for loss of management trust, and defaults at debt-reliant builders.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Scenario map for sizing AI exposure and credit risk.

insights.claim: Markets will lead and accounting will follow on AI surprises, so waiting for write-offs to sell an AI company means acting too late.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Do not use accounting impairments as the exit signal.
insights.quote: waiting to act until accountants write off AI cap ex to sell your AI company implies that you waited too long

insights.claim: The US market and economy have become a giant bet on AI, so success or failure shows up in both write-offs and stock prices.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Passive US equity holders already own the AI bet implicitly.

insights.claim: Investors have four choices on AI: go all-in on AI winning soon, follow market consensus, be a skeptic, or crash out; none permits sitting out the debate.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Pick explicitly rather than inheriting passive exposure.

insights.claim: Betting against AI through shorts and flipping to the disrupted has not worked for most traders in the last two years, and markets can stay irrational longer than an investor can stay solvent.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Shorting the AI trade is a timing-risky stance.
insights.locator: Crash out on the AI story

insights.claim: Damodaran holds five of the Mag Seven and follows market consensus for most of his portfolio, but has put new money mostly in short-term Treasuries yielding about 4% to pass the sleep test.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Practical hedge: keep consensus exposure, fund new money into cash.

insights.claim: Investors who fear AI will disrupt their profession should tilt financial capital away from AI-exposed businesses, since human capital is an unseen portfolio holding; this matters more for younger investors.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Hedge career risk with portfolio allocation.
